text: Publishing works the same way whether you're pushing to Tableau Cloud or Tableau Server. Click Share in the toolbar, choose a project, name the workbook, and for each data source, choose how the server should authenticate to it. That last step is where most of the real decision-making happens.

This is the real publish dialog's Manage Data Sources step, straight from Tableau's own documentation. Allow refresh access lets the server refresh this data using credentials your admin already configured, without ever storing your own password in the workbook. Embed password saves your personal credentials directly into the file — convenient, but anyone with access to that workbook's connection details effectively has your login. Production workbooks should almost always use refresh access.

Publishing a workbook bundles its sheets, dashboards, and usually a data connection together. Publishing a data source on its own means any number of separate workbooks can connect to one shared, governed copy instead of each embedding its own — one refresh schedule, one set of calculations, instead of five slowly drifting copies. Dashboards themselves aren't published separately — they travel with the workbook, and Select Sheets controls which ones viewers actually see.
Next lesson covers what happens after publishing: permissions, scheduled refreshes, subscriptions, and data-driven alerts.
